claims.text: In refractory multiprincipal-element alloys, oxidation resistance and material integrity are controlled by preferential oxidation and formation of a continuous protective oxide scale.
The balance between stable refractory oxides and volatile V-rich oxides determines oxidation resistance.
The Al-Nb-Ti-V-Zr alloy forms V2O5, VO2, TiO2, Nb2O5, and TiNb2O7 during oxidation at 600 °C.
V2O5 is lost through volatility and thereby disrupts the protective oxide scale.
TiO2, Nb2O5, and mixed refractory oxides are stable, slow-growing, and protective.
Stable refractory oxides form an adherent barrier that limits oxygen ingress.
Formation of volatile V-rich oxides produces porous or disrupted scales that accelerate oxidation and loss of material integrity.
Reducing V content will make the oxide scale more adherent and improve oxidation resistance.
Processing-induced chemical ordering can partition refractory elements toward the surface.
Surface enrichment or clustering of refractory elements will favor protective oxide formation.
An alloy with reduced V content or refractory-element surface enrichment will exhibit lower mass gain than the baseline alloy.
An alloy with reduced V content or refractory-element surface enrichment will maintain a more continuous and adherent oxide scale than the baseline alloy.
At 600–700 °C, the baseline Al-Nb-Ti-V-Zr alloy initially follows nearly parabolic oxidation kinetics and later undergoes breakaway oxidation.
At 800–900 °C, the baseline alloy undergoes breakaway oxidation due to scale disruption.
The baseline alloy exhibits increasingly severe oxidation from 600 to 900 °C, culminating in specimen disintegration after 50 hours at 900 °C.
At 900 °C, the oxide scale contains TiNb2O7, AlNbO4, and Nb2Zr6O17.
The proposed volatile-oxide mechanism should govern broadly across high-temperature MPEAs whenever protective and volatile oxide formation compete.
